newsitem.title: UK: UK's Clarks says EMU need not be irrevocable.
newsitem.headline: UK's Clarks says EMU need not be irrevocable.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said on Friday that European monetary union (EMU) need not be irrevocable, although countries joining it should assume that it would be permanent.

"The intention of going into monetary union would be that this is intended to be permanent in the foreseeable future -- that everybody would fix their interest rates together, that everybody would have the same currency," he said on a BBC television phone-in programme.
"Once you've got into that, the idea would be that nobody would come out. In fact, there is never a "never' in politics."
Clarke said previous attempts at monetary union, such as a long-lasting one in southern Europe, had ended.

"We were in monetary union with the Irish Republic for about 50 years. They pulled out of that in the 1970s. So these things can be disentangled. But no-one should go into it believing it was anything other than a lasting situation."

Clarke, the leading Europhile in a Conservative cabinet that contains many "Eurosceptics," said that regardless of which party won the May 1 election, the British people would ultimately have to give their approval in a referendum before the country joined a single currency.
